en.publisherAuthorHTML:
SIR GEORGE ARTHUR

Sir George Compton Archibald Arthur, 3rd Baronet (1860–1946), belonged to the military and courtly world whose most formidable soldier he would later chronicle. A former officer of the 2nd Life Guards, he served during the Great War as Lord Kitchener’s personal private secretary at the War Office, observing at close quarters the responsibilities, working habits and political difficulties of the Field Marshal’s final command.

This proximity determines the character of Life of Lord Kitchener. Arthur did not reconstruct his subject entirely from public despatches after the generation had passed. He had heard the voice, watched the working habits, seen the War Office routine and understood the administrative world in which apparently abstract strategic decisions arrived as memoranda, telegrams, appointments and demands upon men.

He also admired Kitchener. That fact is not a defect to be hidden; it is part of the source.

A near-contemporary biography written by a private secretary inevitably differs from the detached synthesis of a later historian. Arthur knew the personal loyalties, assumptions and language of the world he describes, and his three volumes possess precisely the immediacy later scholarship cannot reproduce.

The present AETERNUS edition therefore treats Arthur’s biography as a historical work of its own age. Its imperial vocabulary, standards of judgement and proximity to Kitchener form part of its documentary value. The editorial task is to illuminate the historical setting without altering the character of the original witness.

The reader should hear the age speaking before being told what later ages thought of it.

en.name: Napoleon Augustus Jennings
en.tagline: Ranger, Reporter and Chronicler of the Border
en.metaDescription: Napoleon Augustus Jennings (1856–1918), author of A Texas Ranger, first published by Charles Scribner’s Sons, New York, 1899. The AETERNUS GREEN SERIES edition is forthcoming.

p: Napoleon Augustus Jennings began life at a considerable distance from the world that would make his name. Born in Philadelphia on 11 January 1856, the son of a prosperous merchant, he was educated at St. Paul’s School in Concord, New Hampshire. At eighteen he left the settled East for Texas and entered a country in which wealth, social position and eastern education mattered rather less than horsemanship, judgment and the ability to make oneself useful.

After early experience among cattlemen, Jennings became associated with Captain Leander McNelly’s Special Force. He remained with the organization until February 1877. The surviving evidence does not speak with one voice about his precise status: later Ranger George Durham described him chiefly as a field clerk, while Texas historical reference works record his joining McNelly’s command. Whatever his formal designation, Jennings knew the men, stories and country closely enough for his recollections to become one of the enduring early narratives of the Special Force.

Following the death of his father, Jennings returned to Philadelphia and attempted to enter the family business. Settled commercial life did not hold him. He went west again and worked at various times as prospector, miner, stagecoach driver and sign painter before discovering the profession that would give permanent form to his powers of observation.
He became a newspaperman.

Jennings worked for newspapers in Philadelphia and New York, later returned to Texas as a reporter for the San Antonio Express, and eventually covered the Mexican Revolution for the New York Herald. Journalism supplied discipline to qualities the frontier had already cultivated: rapid judgment, economy of description and the knowledge that a man may sometimes be revealed more exactly by one sentence of dialogue than by a page of analysis.

Those qualities animate A Texas Ranger. Published by Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1899, the book is neither a formal institutional history nor a neutral chronicle. It is a remembered world shaped by a writer who understood pace, character and anecdote. Contemporary reviewers recognized its vitality; later historians disputed portions of its accuracy. Walter Prescott Webb regarded parts of the narrative with suspicion, while J. Frank Dobie defended its standing among Ranger memoirs, and John H. Jenkins subsequently included it among his Basic Texas Books.

The disagreement is itself revealing. Jennings stands near that unstable boundary between experience and legend where much of the literature of the American frontier was born. He was close enough to the old border to preserve its speech and temper, yet sufficiently removed from it for memory already to have begun arranging experience into story.
He died in New York on 15 December 1918.

By then the Texas of his youth had been transformed by railways, stronger institutions and the closing of the old border conditions. Many of the men he had known were dead, and the Ranger was already passing from mounted officer into national symbol.
Jennings had done what a chronicler of a vanishing world can do.
He had written before the dust had entirely settled.

en.name: George Robert Gleig
en.tagline: Soldier · Clergyman · Military Historian
en.intro: The Reverend George Robert Gleig · Chaplain-General to the Forces
en.metaDescription: George Robert Gleig, soldier, clergyman and military historian; author of Sale’s Brigade in Afghanistan (1846).
en.publisherAuthorHTML:
George Robert Gleig was born at Stirling on 20 April 1796 into a clerical family, but his own early life took a decidedly martial course. After study at Glasgow and Balliol College, Oxford, he abandoned his academic prospects for the Army and entered the 85th Light Infantry, serving during the closing period of the wars against Napoleon and subsequently in the British campaign in North America. He saw active service under Wellington’s military generation and was wounded during the American War.

That experience permanently marked his writing.

Although Gleig later returned to Oxford, took holy orders and pursued a long ecclesiastical career, he never became an armchair military historian. He knew the march, the camp, the strain of campaigning and the habits of soldiers from personal experience. His later appointments included Chaplain-General to the Forces and Inspector-General of Military Schools, while his writings ranged widely across British military and imperial history.

Among his works were accounts of the British campaigns at Washington and New Orleans, studies of Waterloo and Wellington, histories of India and biographies of major imperial figures. Sale’s Brigade in Afghanistan, published by John Murray in London in 1846, belonged naturally within that larger military vocation. The first edition comprised ix + 182 pages and formed part of Murray’s Colonial and Home Library.

Gleig had not himself served in Afghanistan, and he made no pretence of having done so. His authority rested instead upon the evidence he assembled. In his Advertisement he explained that the narrative was drawn chiefly from the manuscript journals of officers engaged in the campaign; he also consulted the Orderly Books of the 13th and drew information from officers personally connected with the events.

This gives the book its particular character.

It is a military narrative written by a combat veteran about a campaign he reconstructed from the records and testimony of other soldiers. Gleig understood the meaning of orders, rear guards, marches, fatigue, fortification and discipline because these were not abstractions to him. His prose consequently moves with an old soldier’s instinct for the practical structure of campaigning.

At the time of publication Sir Robert Sale was already dead.

He had fallen at Moodkee in December 1845 during the First Sikh War, again serving with the Army and again at the front. Gleig closed his preliminary remarks with the knowledge that the commander whose deeds he had gathered could neither approve nor correct the finished narrative.

Yet, as Gleig wrote, “his fame survives him.”

Few episodes justified the phrase more completely than Jellalabad.

LIEUTENANT-GENERAL HENRY DOVETON HUTCHINSON

Companion of the Order of the Star of India

Born 13 September 1847 · baptised at Dinapore, Bengal

Died 21 November 1924, Kensington, London

Soldier · Military Educator · Historian

Henry Doveton Hutchinson belonged to a generation for whom soldiering and the professional study of soldiering were not separate occupations.

Born on 13 September 1847, he entered the Indian military service and developed a career that combined regimental duty, active operations, military education and writing. He served in the Sikkim operations of 1887–88, during the Relief of Chitral in 1895 and in the Tirah campaign of 1897–98. He raised the 2nd Battalion, 3rd Gurkha Rifles in 1891 and later commanded troops in Chitral. From 1896 to 1901 he served as Director of Military Education in India. His later career included duty at the India Office, appointment as Assistant Military Secretary for Indian affairs and service as Director of Staff Duties at the War Office. He eventually retired as a Lieutenant-General and was appointed Companion of the Order of the Star of India.

At the time The Campaign in Tirah appeared in 1898, Hutchinson was a Colonel.

That contemporary rank matters because the book belongs to the middle of his professional life rather than its retrospective end. He was writing not as an elderly memoirist recalling a vanished army, but as an officer still actively engaged in the business of military education.

His bibliography reveals the range of that interest. He wrote upon military sketching, field fortification, Waterloo, Corunna and other campaigns, and later produced regimental history. His concern was consistently practical: how armies understood ground, how men were instructed, how tactical lessons were extracted from experience and how military knowledge might be transmitted before another campaign forced the same lessons to be purchased again.

The Tirah volume occupies a special position within that work.

Its foundations were contemporary.

Hutchinson had contributed letters to The Times while impressions remained fresh and then enlarged the material for book publication with subsequent information. He deliberately avoided converting his introduction into a partisan treatise on frontier policy; instead he sought to provide the general reader sufficient facts to understand the origin of the conflict and then concentrated upon the conduct of the campaign itself.

That professional restraint remains one of the strengths of the book.

Hutchinson is interested in bravery, but also in why an attack succeeded.

He is interested in a regiment, but also in what stood beside it.

He sees a pass as terrain rather than scenery.

He treats transport as a fighting necessity.

The result is a campaign history written by an officer who believed that military experience was wasted unless somebody learned from it.

Hutchinson died on 21 November 1924.

By then the Army he had known had passed through the South African War and the immense transformation of 1914–18.

The lesson beneath his work nevertheless remained intact:

an army that does not study yesterday may be forced to learn it again tomorrow.

en.name: William Robertson
en.tagline: Soldier · Intelligence Officer · Chief of the Imperial General Staff
en.metaDescription: William Robertson (1860–1933), author of From Private to Field-Marshal. The AETERNUS Green Series edition is forthcoming.
en.publisherAuthorHTML:
Soldier

Intelligence Officer

Staff Officer

Chief of the Imperial General Staff

Born 29 January 1860 · Welbourn, Lincolnshire

Died 12 February 1933 · London

William Robert Robertson entered the Army without those advantages that normally shaped an officer’s Victorian career. His father was a tailor and village postmaster. Robertson attended the local school, worked briefly as a pupil-teacher and entered domestic service before deciding to enlist. On 13 November 1877 he joined the 16th (The Queen’s) Lancers.

The regiment became his first university. He qualified in musketry, signalling and elementary intelligence work and rose through the non-commissioned ranks. In 1888 he was commissioned into the 3rd (Prince of Wales’s) Dragoon Guards, an exceptional transition at a time when movement from the ranks into the officer corps remained comparatively rare.

India broadened him from cavalry soldier into professional intelligence officer. Railway transport duties during frontier expeditions were followed by service in the Intelligence Department at Simla. Languages became part of his professional equipment. His journey through Gilgit and the Pamirs in 1894 and his service as Intelligence Officer with the Chitral Relief Force in 1895 placed him within the strategic world of the Great Game at the same time that they developed his practical knowledge of terrain and expeditionary war.

Chitral brought the D.S.O. The Staff College brought something institutionally rarer: Robertson became the first officer risen from the ranks to attend Camberley. South Africa, the War Office and foreign intelligence followed.

His career then accelerated through the machinery of the reformed Army. He became Colonel, Brigadier-General on the General Staff at Aldershot, Major-General and Commandant of the Staff College, and Director of Military Training at the War Office. On the outbreak of the Great War he became Quartermaster-General of the British Expeditionary Force. In 1915 he became Chief of its General Staff, and in December of that year Chief of the Imperial General Staff.

He became a full General in 1916 and served as CIGS until February 1918. His tenure coincided with the great strategic debates of the war: the Western Front, manpower, coalition warfare, the relationship between military and political authority and the allocation of British resources across a global conflict.

Robertson left the CIGS appointment after refusing a strategic command arrangement he believed incompatible with clear responsibility. He subsequently commanded Eastern Command and the Home Forces and in 1919 took over the British Army of the Rhine.

The Crown marked the career repeatedly. Robertson had received the D.S.O. after Chitral, followed by the C.B., C.V.O., K.C.V.O., K.C.B., G.C.B. and G.C.M.G. He was created a Baronet in 1919 and promoted Field-Marshal in March 1920. At the time this memoir appeared in 1921 his proper style was:

Field-Marshal Sir William Robertson, Bart., G.C.B., G.C.M.G., K.C.V.O., D.S.O.

His later G.C.V.O. did not come until 1931.

Robertson later published the much more extensive Soldiers and Statesmen, 1914–1918. But From Private to Field-Marshal remains the more personal book because its true subject is not only the Great War.

It is ascent.

Not ascent as social fantasy, but ascent through work, examination, experience, study and repeated enlargements of responsibility.

No other title in the British military memoir tradition can make the same claim quite so literally.

From Private to Field-Marshal

THE RANKS · THE STAFF · COMMAND

GREEN SERIES · AETERNUS

“Sir William Robertson’s book is necessarily unlike any other which has been written.”

The Spectator, 22 October 1921

No other title in British military autobiography can make quite the same claim.

William Robertson entered the 16th (The Queen’s) Lancers as a trooper in November 1877. Forty-two years later he became a Field-Marshal—the only British soldier to rise from the ranks to the Army’s highest rank.

His memoir carries the reader through the Victorian cavalry, commission into the 3rd (Prince of Wales’s) Dragoon Guards, intelligence service in India, the Pamirs and Chitral, Staff College, the South African War, the War Office and the reform of the British General Staff.

In August 1914 Robertson went to France as Quartermaster-General of the British Expeditionary Force. He sustained its communications during the retreat from Mons, became Chief of the General Staff in 1915 and, later that year, Chief of the Imperial General Staff.

From Whitehall he stood at the centre of Britain’s military direction during the Somme, the campaigns of 1917 and the great strategic disputes over the Western Front, manpower, coalition warfare and political control of military strategy.

His final commands included the Home Forces and the British Army of the Rhine.

en.publisherAuthorHTML:
Major-General Sir Charles Edward Callwell belonged to that notable succession of British officers for whom the practice of war and its systematic study formed complementary occupations.

His military writings included Small Wars: Their Principles and Practice, a work of lasting importance in the literature of expeditionary operations, and studies devoted to the influence of sea power upon land campaigns, the conduct of military expeditions and the wider problems of imperial warfare.

During the Great War he served in the higher machinery of British military administration and acquired direct experience of the competing demands placed upon the War Office by a conflict fought upon several continents.

His authority as a biographer arose not merely from rank or literary accomplishment, but from his familiarity with the professional world in which Sir Stanley Maude had been formed.

The General Who Restored British Arms in Mesopotamia

In April 1916 a British-led army surrendered at Kut. The defeat cast a long shadow over the Mesopotamian campaign and revealed the terrible consequences of an advance undertaken without adequate reserves, transport and supplies.

Eight months later another British and Indian army moved forward along the Tigris.

Its commander was Lieutenant-General Sir Stanley Maude.

A soldier of the Coldstream Guards, a veteran of imperial campaigns and a commander who had served in France and at Gallipoli, Maude possessed the rare faculty of transforming organisation into military power. In Mesopotamia he rebuilt an army whose prestige had been broken, restored its offensive capacity and led it through a deliberate campaign against determined Ottoman resistance.

Kut was recovered. The advance continued. On 11 March 1917 his troops entered Baghdad.

Written by Major-General Sir Charles Edward Callwell, distinguished military theorist and author of Small Wars: Their Principles and Practice, this biography follows Maude from his early regimental service to the achievement which established his enduring place in British military history.

The AETERNUS edition preserves Callwell's original work and frames it with new studies of the Persian Gulf, imperial strategy, the Mesopotamian campaign and the military principles underlying Maude's victory.

MAJOR-GENERAL SIR CHARLES JOHN MELLISS
V.C. · K.C.B. · K.C.M.G.

In 1895
CAPTAIN C. J. MELLISS
9TH BOMBAY INFANTRY

Charles John Melliss was born at Mhow, in Central India, on 12 September 1862, into the military world of British India. He was educated at Wellington College and the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, was commissioned into the East Yorkshire Regiment in 1882 and transferred to the Indian Army two years later.

When Lion-Hunting in Somali-land appeared in 1895 he was a captain in the 9th Bombay Infantry, and it is in that rank that the title page of this edition presents him; the general’s rank, the knighthoods and the Victoria Cross lay in the future. Active service followed almost at once, in East Africa during the M’Wele operations of 1895–96 and on the North-West Frontier in the Kurram Valley and Tirah operations of 1897–98.

In May 1899, bound for West Africa in the steamer Sokoto, he went overboard off Cape Coast Castle after a member of the crew who had fallen into water known for its sharks, and received the bronze medal of the Royal Humane Society. His diary recorded the matter with characteristic dryness: had he not had the constant idea of sharks in his mind, he wrote, he should not have minded the thing a bit.

In the Ashanti campaign of 1900 he served with the West African Frontier Force. At Obassa on 30 September, seeing the enemy gather to stand in the bush, he collected such men as were at hand and led them in a charge into the thick cover. In the hand-to-hand fighting that followed he ran one opponent through with his sword and was shot through the foot by another, but the rush broke the enemy’s position. His Victoria Cross was gazetted on 15 January 1901.

The sporting life exacted its own price in East Africa in 1903, when a lion mauled him so severely that he nearly lost an arm. Promoted lieutenant-colonel in 1906, he commanded the 53rd Sikhs (Frontier Force) until January 1910, a regiment to which he remained attached for the rest of his life and which served in the Zakka Khel operations of 1908; he afterwards held brigade command and was promoted major-general in 1912.

In October 1914 he was given the newly formed 30th Indian Brigade and took it to Mesopotamia. In April 1915 he assumed command at Shaiba, where an Ottoman attack upon the Basra position was met and driven from the field; he fought afterwards on the Euphrates at Nasiriyah and at Ctesiphon, was appointed K.C.B. in October 1915, and shared the siege of Kut-al-Amara until its surrender on 29 April 1916.

Captivity revealed the side of his character that the men remembered longest. On the road north he found British and Indian soldiers left behind by the prisoner columns, sick and starving, and did what his rank still allowed to help them; from Broussa in August 1917 he wrote to the Secretary of State for War that it was beyond his powers of description to convey what he had seen. He was appointed K.C.M.G. in August 1918 for services in Mesopotamia, came home at the end of the war, retired from the Indian Army in 1920 and was honorary colonel of the 53rd Sikhs until 1934. He died at Camberley, Surrey, on 6 June 1936.

The young captain who wrote Lion-Hunting in Somali-land could know none of this. The reader, who does, will find that the knowledge lends the plain confidence of these pages an unusual afterlife.

p: Als Roosevelt im Mai 1889 das Vorwort zum ersten Band von The Winning of the West datierte, war er dreißig Jahre alt. Die Präsidentschaft und die weltpolitische Rolle lagen noch vor ihm.

Geboren 1858 in New York, zwangen ihn Asthma und eine fragile Konstitution früh zu jener Selbstdisziplin, die später zum Lebensprinzip wurde: Widerstand sollte nicht umgangen, sondern überwunden werden.
Roosevelt war kein Historiker im späteren akademischen Sinne. Er war etwas Eigentümlicheres: Gelehrter und politischer Mensch zugleich, Quellenforscher und Erzähler.

Nach dem Tod seiner Frau und seiner Mutter am selben Tag im Februar 1884 kehrte er in das Dakota-Territorium zurück. Der Westen war für ihn fortan kein geographischer Raum mehr, sondern eine historische Schule des Charakters.

Roosevelt wollte erklären, wie aus einem schmalen Streifen englischsprachiger Kolonien an der Atlantikküste ein kontinentales Gemeinwesen wurde. Sein Gegenstand war größer als die Geschichte einzelner Pioniere: ihn interessierte die Bewegung selbst.

en.intro: The author of The Rough Riders, writing before the White House.
en.metaDescription: In 1898 Theodore Roosevelt leaves Washington for Cuba. Cowboys, ranchmen and Eastern athletes become a volunteer regiment whose brief campaign will enter American history. The complete English text of the 1899 first edition, with a new publisher’s apparatus.

portrait.alt: Theodore Roosevelt, after the portrait by Philip Alexius de László, 1908

p: Theodore Roosevelt entered the world in New York City on October 27, 1858, with advantages of family, education and circumstance, but without the physical constitution that later legend might suggest. Severe asthma, bodily weakness and extreme nearsightedness shadowed his childhood. His response was characteristic: he refused to treat weakness as a final verdict.

The famous injunction from his father that he must make his body became, in Roosevelt’s life, something greater than a program of exercise. He came to believe that physical effort, danger, discipline and chosen hardship formed part of moral development. The philosophy he later called the strenuous life grew from this personal revolt against fragility.
Yet Roosevelt was never merely a man of action.

He was a voracious reader, naturalist and historian whose intellectual appetite equaled his physical restlessness. His early The Naval War of 1812 showed a young author already capable of serious documentary work and strategic judgment. Across his lifetime he would write on war, politics, natural history, hunting, exploration, biography and the American West with a productivity unusual even among professional men of letters.

Politics claimed him early. He entered the New York State Assembly in his twenties and quickly became known for reformist combativeness. The trajectory might have remained that of an Eastern political career had private catastrophe not altered its course in 1884, when his mother and his first wife, Alice Lee, died within hours of one another.
Roosevelt went west.

The Dakota Badlands gave him a second education. He ranched, hunted, rode enormous distances, drove cattle and lived among men whose social world differed profoundly from that of New York. The experience did not turn him into a Westerner by birth, nor did he pretend that it had. It did something more important: it taught him to admire a form of practical competence and self-command which he believed modern urban life could too easily weaken.

These years entered his historical imagination as well as his character. Roosevelt would later write the four-volume The Winning of the West, an immense attempt to narrate the continental expansion that had created the republic he knew. By the 1890s, however, the frontier whose advance he had chronicled was itself passing into history.

Roosevelt returned to public life with greater appetite rather than less. He served as United States Civil Service Commissioner, became a New York City Police Commissioner and in 1897 entered the Navy Department as Assistant Secretary. In each office he showed the same impatience with inert machinery. He expected systems to function and men entrusted with public responsibilities to discharge them visibly.

At the Navy Department this instinct acquired strategic weight. Roosevelt believed that the United States could not enter the coming century as a major nation while neglecting sea power. He pushed preparedness, modernization and a conception of national power larger than coastal defense.
Then came war.

Roosevelt had advocated preparedness in Washington; now he refused to let other men bear the entire physical burden of the policy he supported. On May 6, 1898, he left office and accepted a commission as lieutenant colonel of the First United States Volunteer Cavalry.
The decision itself is important, but so is the rank he accepted.

Roosevelt might have sought the colonelcy. Instead he supported Leonard Wood for command because Wood possessed the professional experience necessary to organize the regiment quickly. Roosevelt understood that enthusiasm, however fierce, did not replace technical knowledge. He intended to learn under a man better prepared for the immediate task.
This was not modesty in the conventional sense.
It was judgment.

In Cuba, that judgment would be tested alongside everything else. At Las Guasimas Roosevelt encountered sustained enemy fire for the first time. When Wood advanced to brigade command, Roosevelt took over the regiment and later received the colonelcy formally.
Then came July 1.

The attack upon Kettle Hill and the San Juan positions would become the central military image of Roosevelt’s life, yet what matters beneath the image is the alignment between his public creed and his personal conduct. Roosevelt had spent years praising vigor, courage and willingness to assume responsibility. On the battlefield he placed himself where the consequences of those words applied to him as directly as to the men he commanded.
That fact gave the episode unusual political force.
The Cuban campaign did not create Roosevelt’s character. It certified it in public.

Within months he was elected Governor of New York. In 1900 he was elected Vice President, and after William McKinley’s assassination in September 1901 the forty-two-year-old Roosevelt entered the White House.

The presidency revealed a range no single battlefield image could contain. Roosevelt confronted corporate power, enlarged the practical authority of the presidency, intervened in labor conflict, advanced the Panama Canal, strengthened the Navy and pursued an American foreign policy based upon the conviction that diplomacy carried greater weight when backed by visible capability.

He also became one of the decisive presidential figures in the history of American conservation. The hunter and former ranchman did not conclude that wilderness existed merely to be consumed. He believed that forests, waters, wildlife and open country formed part of the national inheritance and required deliberate protection from short-term exhaustion.
This combination of hunter, conservationist, soldier and peacemaker appears contradictory only if each role is reduced to a caricature.
Roosevelt himself saw a common principle.
Power imposed duty.

The strong man had obligations precisely because he possessed strength; the strong nation likewise. Preparedness was not valuable because war was desirable, but because helplessness surrendered the decision to others.
In 1906 this philosophy reached an extraordinary counterpart to San Juan when Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War.

His own military honor remained unresolved during his lifetime. Roosevelt had been recommended for the Medal of Honor after Santiago, but the decoration was not awarded. More than a century after the charge, in 2001, it was conferred posthumously for his actions of July 1, 1898.
Thus two distinctions of very different character stand over his name: the Medal of Honor and the Nobel Peace Prize.

They describe not two Roosevelts, but the breadth of one conception of public life. Courage mattered when bullets were close. Restraint and judgment mattered when nations possessed the power to kill on a far greater scale.
The Rough Rider became President.
The field enlarged.
The requirement to bear responsibility remained.

de.intro: Senator, Konsul, Prokonsul der Provinz Asia und der schärfste Beobachter des frühen Prinzipats: Tacitus schrieb die Geschichte der Kaiser von Tiberius bis Nero als Mann aus der Mitte der Macht — kalt, verknappt, ohne Rücksicht auf den Ruf der Herrschenden.

de.bioLede: Er sah Senatoren schweigen, schmeicheln und fallen; er erlebte, wie das Wort im Senat zur Gefahr wurde. Aus dieser Erfahrung gewann seine Geschichtsschreibung ihre Kraft.

p: Cornelius Tacitus wurde wohl um 56 n. Chr. geboren; sein Geburtsort ist nicht sicher überliefert. Unter den flavischen Kaisern durchlief er die Ämterlaufbahn, war 97 Suffektkonsul und verwaltete später als Prokonsul die Provinz Asia.

Er kannte die Mechanismen des Prinzipats aus eigener Anschauung — die Denunziationen unter Domitian ebenso wie die vorsichtige Öffnung unter Nerva und Trajan. Seine großen Werke, die Historien und die Annalen, entstanden in dieser späten Zeit. Er starb vermutlich nach 117.

Wo Cicero die harmonische, ausbalancierte Periode suchte, schuf Tacitus ein dunkles, monumentales Latein: asymmetrisch, überraschend, voller Auslassungen und jäher Wendungen. Verblose Ellipsen, harte Antithesen und peitschenhiebartige Sentenzen legen die Nacktheit der Macht offen.
Seine Sprache gleicht dem Staat, den er beschreibt — unberechenbar, gefährlich, ohne leeren Prunk. Die Aeternus-Ausgabe stellt dem Leser diese brevitas nicht geglättet gegenüber.

Von den Annalen, der Geschichte Roms vom Tod des Augustus bis in die letzten Jahre Neros, sind zwölf Bücher erhalten: die Bücher I–VI und XI–XVI. Die Bücher VII–X sind verloren und werden nicht rekonstruiert; Lücken der Überlieferung bleiben im Lesetext sichtbar.

p: Felix Salten wuchs in Wien auf. Als Journalist, Theaterkritiker und Schriftsteller gehörte er zum Umfeld des Jungen Wien. Er schrieb über Kunst und Bühne ebenso wie über das Leben auf den Straßen der Stadt.
1939 floh er mit seiner Frau in die Schweiz. Seinen Lebensabend verbrachte er in Zürich, wo er 1945 starb.
In Bambi wird der Wald aus der Nähe eines jungen Rehs erfahrbar: die erste Wiese, die Stimmen der Nachbarn, das Vertrauen zur Mutter. Mit den Jahreszeiten wächst auch Bambis Erfahrung.
Bambi ist der Auftakt unserer editorischen Arbeit an Saltens Tierwelt; Bambis Kinder führt sie fort.

Walt Disneys Zeichentrickfilm von 1942 hat das Bild von Bambi weltweit geprägt. Saltens Roman besitzt seinen eigenen Ton und seine eigenen Gestalten. Gobo und das Gespräch der beiden Herbstblätter gehören zu den Begegnungen, die den Lesern des Buches vorbehalten bleiben.

Das düstere Vermächtnis des großen Wald-Epos Die Fortsetzung des Weltbestsellers — 1940 in deutscher Sprache erschienen.

Mit Bambis Kinder schuf Felix Salten im Schatten des heraufziehenden Zweiten Weltkriegs die unerbittliche Fortsetzung seines legendären Meisterwerks. Der Wald ist nicht friedlicher geworden: Bambis und Falines Zwillinge, der ängstliche Geno und die stolze Gurri, müssen sich in einer Schöpfung behaupten, die von Gefahren, Hunger und der ewigen Lauer des namenlosen Jägers durchsetzt ist.

Als Gurri in die Hände des Menschen gerät und Rettung in Gefangenschaft umschlägt, tritt Bambi – nun der unnahbare Fürst des Forstes – aus den Schatten. Seine Lehre kennt keine Kompromisse: Wer in der Wildnis überleben will, darf sich niemals der Macht unterwerfen.

Eine bibliophile Prachtausgabe des deutschen Originaltexts — veredelt durch meisterhafte, bildgewaltige Neuinterpretationen von atemberaubender räumlicher Tiefe.

de.bioLede: Carlo Collodi ist der Künstlername des italienischen Schriftstellers Carlo Lorenzini. Seine Geschichte einer Holzpuppe erschien 1883 als Buch.

p: Bevor Pinocchio durch spätere Bearbeitungen zur bloßen Kinderbuchfigur wurde, schuf Carlo Collodi 1883 eine der vielschichtigsten Parabeln der europäischen Literatur. Seine Holzpuppe ist kein angepasstes Kind, sondern ein eigensinniger Rebell, der sich zunächst jeder Ordnung, Arbeit und Einsicht verweigert.

In einer Welt von Armut, Täuschung und strengen Gesetzen muss die Figur am eigenen Leib erfahren, dass Freiheit ohne Verantwortung keine Heimat findet. Vom frühen Ende der sprechenden Grille über die Bedrohung an der Großen Eiche bis hin zu den Irrwegen im Spielzeugland zeigt Collodis Original unbeschönigt die Mühen und die Würde des Erwachsenwerdens.

de.bioLede: Banastre Tarleton schrieb aus der Perspektive des britischen Offiziers, der im Süden der amerikanischen Kolonien zugleich gefürchtet, bewundert und heftig angefeindet wurde.

p: Als Kommandeur der British Legion führte Tarleton eine hochmobile Truppe aus loyalistischer Kavallerie und leichter Infanterie durch die Karolinas und Virginia. Sein Name wurde mit der Härte dieses Kriegsschauplatzes verbunden.
Der Bericht verfolgt den Feldzug von 1780 und 1781 aus britischer Sicht und reicht von Charleston und Camden über Cowpens und Guilford Court House bis in die Schlussphase vor Yorktown.
Tarleton veröffentlichte das Werk 1787 in London. Es ist weder spätes Bekenntnis noch distanzierte Geschichtsschreibung, sondern eine präzise und parteiliche Rechtfertigung des eigenen Handelns.

Besondere Schärfe erhält das Buch durch Tarletons Auseinandersetzung mit Lord Cornwallis. Die im Anhang abgedruckten Briefe, Befehle und Berichte machen den Band zugleich zu einer umfangreichen Quellensammlung.

Die deutsche Ausgabe folgt vollständig der Londoner Erstausgabe von 1787. Sie enthält alle fünf Karten und Pläne, die Anmerkungen des Verfassers sowie sämtliche von Tarleton abgedruckten Schriftstücke.

de.bioLede: Aus den Schweizer Voralpen und der Erfahrung städtischer Enge entstand ein Werk über Heimat, Verlust, Heilung und tätige Nächstenliebe.

p: Johanna Louise Heusser wurde am 12. Juni 1827 im schweizerischen Hirzel am Zürichsee geboren. Als Tochter eines Landarztes und einer pietistisch geprägten Dichterin wuchs sie mit genauer Kenntnis der bäuerlichen Welt der Voralpen auf.

Nach der Heirat mit dem Zürcher Stadtschreiber Johann Bernhard Spyri lebte sie in Zürich. Die Spannung zwischen Bergwelt und Stadt, Geborgenheit und seelischer Enge prägte später die dramatische Bewegung von Heidi.

1880 erschien Heidis Lehr- und Wanderjahre, 1881 folgte Heidi kann brauchen, was es gelernt hat. Erst gemeinsam schließen beide Bände den Bogen von der Trennung über die Heimkehr bis zur Weitergabe des Empfangenen.

AETERNUS legt beide Teile ungekürzt nach den Erstausgaben vor. Rechtschreibung und Satzführung sind behutsam modernisiert; Schweizer Sprachkolorit, religiöse Ernsthaftigkeit und der Wortlaut des Originals bleiben erhalten.
Spyri begann erst mit über vierzig Jahren zu veröffentlichen. Ihr Werk umfasst mehr als dreißig Bände; Heidi machte sie weltweit bekannt.
Sie mied das Rampenlicht bis an ihr Lebensende und starb am 7. Juli 1901 in Zürich.

de.bioLede: Kiplings Werk verbindet die Präzision des Zeitungsreporters mit einem musikalischen Gehör für Stimmen, Rituale und die unerbittlichen Rhythmen der Natur.

p: Rudyard Kipling wurde 1865 in Bombay als Kind britischer Eltern geboren. Nach einer harten Erziehungszeit in England kehrte er 1882 als Siebzehnjähriger nach Nordindien zurück.

Als Lokalreporter der Civil and Military Gazette in Lahore und später für The Pioneer in Allahabad schärfte er seinen Blick für technische Einzelheiten, soziale Schichtungen und die vielen Stimmen des kolonialen Alltags.
Nach seiner Heirat mit Caroline Balestier lebte Kipling im ländlichen Vermont. In dem von ihm entworfenen Haus Naulakha schrieb er 1894 und 1895 die beiden Dschungelbücher.

Die Wälder Seonis entstanden aus räumlicher Distanz und verdichteter Erinnerung. Ihr Dschungel ist kein botanisches Abbild, sondern eine Welt von Hunger und Schutz, Zugehörigkeit und Ausstoßung, Gesetz und gefährlicher Freiheit.

1907 erhielt Kipling als erster englischsprachiger Autor und damals jüngster Preisträger den Nobelpreis für Literatur. Gewürdigt wurden seine Beobachtungskraft, die Originalität seiner Vorstellung und die Kraft seiner Erzählkunst.

Sein Erbe bleibt mit dem viktorianischen Imperialismus verbunden. Die Ausgabe bewahrt diese historische Spannung: sprachliche Energie und Naturmythos stehen neben Hierarchie, Herrschaftsanspruch und den Widersprüchen des britischen Empire.

de.eyebrow: Blau · Wirtschaft, Industrie und die Titanen des Fortschritts
de.intro: Artillerieoffizier, Erfinder, Unternehmer: Werner von Siemens baute aus einer Berliner Hinterhauswerkstatt ein Weltunternehmen und legte mit dem dynamoelektrischen Prinzip den Grund für die Starkstromtechnik. Seine Lebenserinnerungen erzählen diesen Weg aus erster Hand.
de.metaDescription: Werner von Siemens: Leben, Werk und die neue Ausgabe seiner Lebenserinnerungen nach der Erstausgabe von 1892 in der Blauen Reihe des Aeternus Verlags.
de.ogDescription: Der Architekt des elektrischen Zeitalters. Leben und Werk von Werner von Siemens.
de.bioLede: Als er 1816 geboren wurde, reiste eine Nachricht mit Pferd und Schiff. Als er 1892 starb, verbanden Telegraphendrähte und Tiefseekabel Europa mit Indien und Amerika.

p: Werner Siemens wurde am 13. Dezember 1816 in Lenthe bei Hannover geboren, als viertes von vierzehn Kindern einer Gutspächterfamilie. Die preußische Artillerie öffnete ihm den Weg an die Berliner Artillerie- und Ingenieurschule, wo er zwischen 1835 und 1838 seine naturwissenschaftlich-technische Ausbildung erhielt.

1847 gründete er mit dem Mechaniker Johann Georg Halske die Telegraphen-Bauanstalt Siemens & Halske. Mit seinen Brüdern Wilhelm in London und Carl in Petersburg wuchs daraus ein Haus, dessen Linien vom Kaukasus bis nach Indien und über den Atlantik reichten.

1866 fand Siemens das dynamoelektrische Prinzip: eine Maschine, die elektrische Energie in wirtschaftlich nutzbarer Größe erzeugte. Damit begann der Übergang von der Nachrichten- zur Starkstromtechnik.

Er wirkte zugleich als Abgeordneter, trat für ein wirksames Patentwesen ein und setzte sich für die Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt ein. 1888 wurde er in den erblichen Adelsstand erhoben; er starb am 6. Dezember 1892 in Charlottenburg.

Zwischen 1889 und 1892 schrieb Siemens seine Lebenserinnerungen: Festungshaft und erste Experimente, Telegraphenlinien und Kabelschiffe, Brüder, Mitarbeiter und Konkurrenten, Irrtümer ebenso wie Erfolge.
Die Aeternus-Ausgabe folgt der Erstausgabe von Julius Springer, Berlin 1892, ungekürzt und in heutiger Rechtschreibung, mit Frontispiz, Tafeln, Zeittafel, Nachwort und Register.
